newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia watchdog investigates soccer-drug links.
newsitem.headline: Colombia watchdog investigates soccer-drug links.

text.p: Drug traffickers control 80 percent of Colombia's top five soccer clubs and have stakes in many others, the head of the country's corporate watchdog said on Thursday.

In the first systematic probe of its kind, the Companies Superintendency investigated 100,000 shareholders of all of Colombia's professional soccer teams. It believes a group of "between 50 and 80" people are pumping proceeds from cocaine and heroin trafficking into the country's most popular sport.

"(Illicit money) is really a euphemism and there are many things that suggest that these funds invested in (some) clubs are linked to drug trafficking," Companies Superintendent Dario Laguado told Reuters, confirming media reports that drug interests control about 80 percent of the top five clubs.

Superintendency officials say the clubs most tainted by drug money are America from the city of Cali, Millionarios from capital Bogota, Atletico Nacional from Medellin, Deportivo Cali and Envigado. At least 15 smaller regional teams are also suspected of drug links.

Millionarios directors were unavailable for comment on Thursday. Atlectico Nacional manager Juan Guillermo Montoya said he "welcomed" the probe and added: "We don't have any problem in that respect." Envigado manager Javier Velasquez criticised news reports of the probe as "sensationalist" and said "this type of investigation is damaging to the reputation of clubs and their directors."

Laguardo said 174 soccer shareholders had either failed to explain the source of the cash they invested in soccer clubs or could not be fully identified -- raising suspicions that some may be aliases for known drug lords.

The final report will be completed this month and the results will be passed to the Chief Prosecutor's office, which has already opened a preliminary investigation, a spokesman said. Clubs could face hefty sanctions if they are found to be financed with drug money and individuals could have their shares confiscated under a recently introduced asset stripping law if they are found to have links with narco-trafficking.

Bogota's second soccer club, Santa Fe, was not directly mentioned by the superintendency but its director Cesar Villegas was arrested last year and is under investigation for illicit enrichment from drug trafficking, the spokesman said.

Laguardo gave few details on the "suspicious" shareholders but said the widow of Gonzalo Rodriguez Gacha, late head of the Medellin drug mob's military operations, had a minority stake in Millionarios. Her husband was said to have a major holding in the club before he was killed by police in 1989.

The links between Colombia's drug cartels and the "beautiful game" stem back to the early 1980s. Despite the findings of his investigation, Laguardo believes the game is "much cleaner" than it has been for most of the past 15 years.

He said that the death or capture of all of Colombia's top drug barons meant their stakes had passed to their heirs and many had been sold to legitimate investors, including major corporate sponsors. The head of the now defunct Medellin cartel, Pablo Escobar, and the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers, jailed leaders of the Cali cartel, were all said to have major holdings in soccer clubs.

"Soccer stars fell victim to the mafia. They were bought, they were promoted and they were murdered," Simon Strong wrote in "Whitewash," his history of the Colombia cocaine trade. "(Soccer teams) reflected power and social status ... and were big business. They offered ways to launder money in Colombia and abroad," he added.

Many sports analysts believe it was financing from drug cartels that led to the Colombian national team's rise to glory in the run-up to the 1994 World Cup in the United States. Despite being favourites to win, Colombia had a disastrous showing that ended with the murder of defender Andres Escobar shortly after he returned to Medellin.
